# Integrix methods (auto-generated example from the demo run)

## Methods: tri-omics integration (Omnix Integrix 1.0.0)

Transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics data were integrated with Omnix Integrix (tri-omics integration (transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics)). The contrast was Tumor versus Control; tier 1 - paired: the same samples are measured in every layer. Data were log2-transformed where needed, features missing in more than 50% of samples in every group were removed and remaining missing values were imputed with the feature minimum minus one log2 unit. Batch effects were corrected within each layer only, with the group effect protected.

Per-layer differential statistics were moderated t-statistics with empirical-Bayes variance shrinkage (Smyth 2004), converted to signed z-scores so that layers on different scales are integrated on a common scale. Gene-protein concordance was assessed by orthogonal (Deming) regression of protein on mRNA z-scores and a per-gene discordance statistic; within-sample coupling was the Spearman correlation of group-centred mRNA and protein levels.

Genes, proteins and metabolites were mapped to the Human-GEM genome-scale metabolic model (knowledge base integrix-kb-2026-10-30) by Ensembl, UniProt, symbol, HMDB, KEGG, ChEBI or name. For every observable reaction (at least one measured enzyme and one measured non-currency metabolite; transport, exchange and pool reactions excluded) enzyme evidence E was obtained from protein z-scores through the gene-protein-reaction rule (AND = complex, minimum absolute evidence with sign agreement; OR = isozymes, abundance-weighted mean), using mRNA z-scores scaled by the observed mRNA-protein coupling when the protein was not measured. The metabolite balance M was the difference between the mean z-score of products and of substrates divided by sqrt(2), and reaction coherence was C = E x M.

Statistical significance was calibrated by 1000 sample-label permutations applied jointly to all layers (preserving cross-omics dependence of matched samples) and by 1000 topology permutations that shuffle measured values among nodes of similar network degree. P-values for C were computed from the product-normal distribution with location, scale and correlation estimated from the permutations; q-values used the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. A reaction was called coherent when both label and topology q < 0.05. Interpretive patterns (e.g. candidate bottleneck, non-abundance regulation) were assigned with a |z| threshold of 1.5 and describe associations, not causal mechanisms.

Pathway activity per layer was the Stouffer sum of member z-scores standardised against the label permutations; layers were combined by a weighted Stouffer test, heterogeneity was assessed by Cochran's Q and I2, and pathways were classified as shared-concordant, shared-discordant or omics-specific. Pathways with fewer than 3 measured members in a layer were labelled not assessable in that layer. Reporter metabolites (Patil & Nielsen 2005) summarised the coherence of reactions around each metabolite.

References: Robinson et al., Sci Signal 2020 (Human-GEM); Smyth, Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol 2004; Patil & Nielsen, PNAS 2005; Yeh et al., Genome Res 2004; Kolde et al., Bioinformatics 2012; Argelaguet et al., Genome Biol 2020; Singh et al., Bioinformatics 2019; Benjamini & Hochberg, JRSS-B 1995.
